newsitem.title: GERMANY: German opposition blasts Waigel on finance policy.
newsitem.headline: German opposition blasts Waigel on finance policy.

text.p: Germany's opposition parties blasted Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Wednesday in a bitter emergency parliamentary debate, accusing the government of being too divided to carry out urgently needed reforms.

Many speakers cited searing criticism of the government in Tuesday's report by six leading economic institutes, who also predicted Germany would not meet the Maastricht criteria in 1997 for participation in Europe's planned single currency.

But Waigel pledged the government's budget deficit would be held below the 3.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) required to take part in the currency union, despite lower tax revenues and higher outlays for unemployment than planned.
"Your main problem is not the opposition. It's your inability to act as a coalition," Greens party parliamentary leader Joschka Fischer told the government.

Rudolf Scharping, parliamentary leader of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), said a recent tax row the coalition parties fought out in the media showed they were incapable of acting sensibly together.

"We can't let policy be decided by war of interviews between coalition partners," said Scharping, whose party called the debate, forcing several parliamentarians accompanying Chancellor Helmut Kohl on a tour of Asia to fly back to Bonn.
The SPD accused Kohl's government of maintaining an unjust tax system, running up debts and doing little to help the country's four million unemployed get a job.

Waigel hit back, accusing it of wasting taxpayers' money by bringing deputies back to Bonn for the debate. "On the one hand you support Maastricht while with the other you block the necessary consolidation of spending," he added.
The SPD used its majority in the upper chamber earlier this month to block government plans to delay a rise in child benefit payments.

To fill the gap, the government decided to postpone a cut in the hated "solidarity surcharge" levied to help rebuild eastern Germany. The move brought Kohl's coalition to the brink of collapse by provoking the ire of the liberal Free Democrats, who had long fought for the cut.
Waigel said the opposition could not deflect him from ensuring Germany met its financial targets, with the 1997 budget deficit not exceeding the planned 56.5 billion marks ($37 billion).
He conceded, however, Bonn had to make a small extra payment for the Federal Labour Office for 1997 and that tax income would probably be lower than originally hoped.
But he faced heavy fire from opposition members who also quoted from critical commentaries on government policy from normally friendly newspapers.
"We could fill this entire debate just by reading from conservative newspapers," said SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine.
Fischer quoted from a damning front-page editorial in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung daily which said: "The consequences of indecision and populism are now clear to see.
"Western Germany is creaking under the weight of reforming eastern Germany while the east develops into the most expensive economic disaster of the postwar era."
The coalition's majority defeated an SPD motion asserting Germany had moved out of "economic equlibrium". ($1=1.5086 Mark)
